Building

Verdnt Group

I co-founded Verdnt Group with Diego Sanchez Tirado. We’re building Verdnt Studio, a tool for food and drink teams developing new drinks. The goal is to help them turn market research into product ideas they can test.

Co-founder

A closer look

Verdnt Studio brings together research from social media and retail shelves to help teams decide what to make next. I work with clients to understand what they need and build the software.

Our client work includes software that combines market research with a company’s product information to suggest new products. Teams can check the sources behind each suggestion before deciding what to test.

Visit Verdnt Group

Trus

I co-founded Trus with Diego Sanchez Tirado to help people create software for their own work. The idea was to describe what you needed and have AI build a workspace for it. Trus is now retired.

Co-founder · Retired

A closer look

I helped build the first version, where AI assembled workspaces from a set of tables, charts, calendars, and other components we had built.

I later focused on product direction and finding customers, while Diego led the engineering.

Strategy

Find the niche the incumbent ignores.

HyperPay is a payment processor in a crowded market. Instead of pitching a better payment product, we looked at the cash merchants leave sitting idle. The working-capital advance was the idea the judges liked.

From: HyperPay case competition, 2026

Check that the audience exists before you build.

I built Forge, an incubator for student nonprofits, before I knew anyone wanted it. We had to cut it back. At FStea I pushed to aim the drink at college students, because that’s where it already fit. Now I try to find out whether people want something before I build more of it.

From: Homer Humanities and FStea

Find the bottleneck before solving everything.

Trus started as a huge, vague idea: you describe the software you need and AI assembles it. We started getting somewhere when we picked one problem, how long each generated piece took to appear, and worked on that first. I tend to let scope grow, so now I decide early which parts get my time and which stay small.

From: Trus

Commit to a decision, then say what you’d watch.

Most real decisions get made with incomplete data, and waiting longer usually doesn’t change that. So I pick a path and say why. Then I name the risks I can see and what I’ll check next.

From: my interview notes, and economics

A problem gets fixable once you can measure it.

At FStea I kept a spreadsheet with a row for every campus store that sold the drink. With the numbers in one place, the team could see which moves were working. I also learned to check the denominator first, because a unit price per case and a unit price per bottle are easy to mix up.

From: FStea, 2025, and Verdnt client work

Tech & AI

On my own time, I run a small team of AI agents that handle my coding and notes.

Use the model to interpret, and code for anything that has to be right.

In a quoting product, a wrong answer costs real money. A language model is good at reading a messy part description, so that’s the job I give it. The pricing math stays in plain code, with a check on top that tells me when something went wrong.

From: Camber, 2026

A model can sound sure and still be wrong.

I never let a model’s confidence decide on its own whether something ships. My Camber demo answers a deliberately vague request with “REVIEW REQUIRED” instead of guessing. I want software to say so when it isn’t sure.

From: the Camber homepage demo

A tool only helps if people trust it.

At Morgan Stanley, the agents I built were only useful once analysts understood how they worked, so I put as much effort into explaining them to non-technical colleagues as into the code. At Verdnt, every suggestion shows its sources, so anyone can check where a recommendation came from, ours included.

From: Morgan Stanley and Verdnt Group

Check what should have been there and wasn’t.

When I built my own job-search pipeline, almost every bug was a silent drop: a real posting lost to a broken source or a filter that was too strict. Checking the results didn’t catch those. Now I also check for postings that should have shown up and didn’t.

From: a personal automation project, 2026

AI is a tool, and people stay responsible for it.

I want to build AI that helps people do more, rather than AI that replaces them. In the winning Stanford policy memo I co-wrote, our part proposed short in-person checks where students explain their reasoning out loud.

From: philosophy coursework and the Stanford memo, 2026

Values

Consistent, unglamorous work compounds.

Volunteering with the Ethical Culture Society, I wrote cards, made sandwiches and helped with donation drives. I found I do some of my best work as a reliable teammate, when someone else is in charge.

From: volunteering in Silicon Valley

Finish what you start.

At work I care about doing my own part properly and about the people I work with. I also try to carry ideas and commitments all the way through. When something goes wrong, I tell the right person early and say what I plan to do.

From: my interview notes

No fate, only action and reaction.

That’s the rule in Statesman, the board game I designed. It’s also close to how I think about my own choices. My philosophy essays keep coming back to the idea that a choice can be voluntary and still shaped by past experience. Schopenhauer put it this way: “Man can do what he wills but he cannot will what he wills.”

From: Statesman and my essays on free will

Watch the tape.

When I coached karate, I filmed my students’ sparring rounds and went through them technique by technique, looking for the one thing to fix. I go through a spreadsheet the same way now.

From: coaching at Okaigan Karate

What I put first.

When I wrote down what I value most, I named three things: the people close to me, my health, and the work.

From: a note to myself, 2026

Books

The unread books on my shelf are a reminder of what I don’t know and might yet discover. These are the ones I’ve read and still think about, with a note on what I took from each.

My Brilliant Friend

No legal or family tie holds Elena and Lila together. They keep choosing the friendship, over and over. Ferrante makes what they leave unsaid as loud as what they say.

Elena Ferrante · my favorite novel

Diagnostic Political Philosophy

Sluga asks how to decide well without the full picture, which is what governing takes when misinformation is everywhere. I ran into the same question in economics, where most real decisions get made with incomplete data.

Hans Sluga · I helped research and edit it

Beyond Good and Evil

I read it across a desk from Professor Sluga in our weekly meetings. He always had another question ready, so I learned to show up having read chapter twelve.

Friedrich Nietzsche · read with Hans Sluga

The Order of Things

I helped build more than 200 pages of material for Sluga’s graduate seminar on it. Writing for graduate students, I had to break each hard idea into steps someone else could follow.

Michel Foucault · seminar material

Three books on meritocracy

I read them side by side for a Stanford writing class. Together they show how often institutions redefine merit, and how much the definition decides who wins. Kirn also writes about the gap between performing competence and having it. I still haven’t settled what merit should be.

Sandel, The Tyranny of Merit · Markovits, The Meritocracy Trap · Kirn, Lost in the Meritocracy

Republic and Apology

What I took from them was the allegory of the cave and the case for the examined life. Plato’s city run by philosopher-kings became the premise of Statesman, the board game I designed.

Plato · UChicago summer program, 2022
